item.title: Scramjet Flame Stabilization: How Pilot Injection Switches Modes
item.description: This paper investigates the influence of pilot hot gas injection on flame stabilization within a cavity-based scramjet combustor. The authors…
item.content:encoded:
Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 68/100

This paper investigates the influence of pilot hot gas injection on flame stabilization within a cavity-based scramjet combustor. The authors employed three-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations to model ethylene fuel injection in a dual-solution regime, where two distinct flame stabilization modes could exist. The primary goal was to understand how pilot injection, at varying heating levels, affects both ignition and sustained flame stabilization, particularly focusing on potential mode transitions.

The simulations revealed that flame stabilization is highly sensitive to the pilot heating power. A low level of pilot heating maintained the flame in a cavity shear-layer stabilization mode. However, when the pilot heating was sufficiently high, it induced a transition to a jet-wake stabilization mode. This transition was primarily attributed to a reduction in the ignition delay within the unburned jet-wake region, caused by the elevated temperatures from the pilot. Additionally, pilot injection was found to enhance fuel–air mixing through the generation of vortices, with both the reduced ignition delay and mixing enhancement intensifying as the pilot heating power increased. Consequently, high heating power facilitated upstream flame propagation and flow separation, which ultimately triggered the observed mode transition. A theoretical analysis, based on Semenov thermal ignition theory, supported these findings by showing that high pilot heating promoted chemical heat release in the unburned jet-wake, exceeding the enthalpy outflow of the initial cavity shear-layer mode, leading to a sustained temperature rise and initiating the transition.

Understanding these flame stabilization mode transitions is important for the design and operation of scramjet engines. The ability to control or predict such transitions through pilot injection strategies directly impacts the reliability and performance envelope of high-speed propulsion systems, which are critical for applications like high-speed missiles.

Reference

  1. Xu Zhang, Lianjie Yue, Dehai Yu et al., “Flame Stabilization Mode Transition Induced by Pilot Injection in a Cavity-Based Scramjet,” AIAA Journal, 2026-03-01. Link

item.title: Comparing Stability Codes for Hypersonic Cone Heating in High Enthalpy Flows
item.description: This paper presents a comparative analysis of several boundary-layer stability codes applied to hypersonic, high-enthalpy flows over blunted cones….
item.content:encoded:
Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 75/100

This paper presents a comparative analysis of several boundary-layer stability codes applied to hypersonic, high-enthalpy flows over blunted cones. The study focuses on two geometries: a 7-degree and a 10.9-degree half-angle blunted cone. The primary objective is to assess the influence of different numerical approaches on second-mode instability and to characterize the role of high-temperature gas effects. The computational results from seven distinct stability codes are compared against experimental data obtained from the High Enthalpy Shock Tunnel (HIEST) in Japan and the High-Enthalpy Laboratory Munich (HELM) in Germany.

The analysis quantifies the impact of high-temperature gas effects on the second mode and investigates the influence of uncertainties, such as minor variations in mean-flow conditions or wall temperature. A specific comparison is also performed between air and CO2 test gases, highlighting differences in stability characteristics under varying gas compositions. The paper provides insights into the agreement and discrepancies among the various computational methods and their ability to reproduce experimental observations under high-enthalpy conditions.

This work is significant for the aerothermodynamics community as it enhances confidence in computational tools used for predicting boundary-layer stability and transition on high-speed vehicles. A better understanding of second-mode instability and real gas effects in high-enthalpy flows is crucial for accurate aerodynamic heating predictions and the design of effective thermal protection systems for hypersonic missiles and reentry vehicles.

This paper review was generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash and curated by AeroSentinel v2.5.0.

Reference

  1. Viola Wartemann, Joseph Kuehl, Tony Liang et al., “Stability Analysis for High-Enthalpy Cone Experiments in HELM and HIEST Facilities,” AIAA Journal, 2026-02-22. Link

item.title: Controlling Supersonic STBLI with Ridge Roughness: LES Insights
item.description: This paper investigates the effectiveness of spanwise heterogeneous, ridge-type wall roughness in passively controlling shock-wave/turbulent…
item.content:encoded:
Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 65/100

This paper investigates the effectiveness of spanwise heterogeneous, ridge-type wall roughness in passively controlling shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interactions (STBLIs). The authors employed wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) to analyze a Mach 2.0 impinging STBLI flow with a 40-degree impinging-shock angle. They considered incoming turbulent boundary layers at two friction Reynolds numbers, approximately 350 and 1200, and explored multiple roughness configurations scaled by either inner or outer flow parameters.

The results indicate that while the rough-wall configurations introduce a moderate increase in mean drag, they substantially alter the dynamics of the interaction. The wall-pressure fluctuations near the separation-shock foot, which consist of low-frequency components from large-scale shock excursions and high-frequency components from amplified turbulence, were significantly attenuated. At the lower Reynolds number, both low- and high-frequency components contributed comparably to the overall reduction. At the higher Reynolds number, a stronger overall reduction of the pressure fluctuation peak was observed, primarily due to the effective suppression of the low-frequency component. Cross-correlation analyses suggest downstream mechanisms drive the low-frequency dynamics in this strong interaction regime, where large-scale shock excursions are mainly driven by the breathing of the reverse-flow bubble. Large-scale Görtler-like vortices were identified around the reattachment location in all cases, appearing largely unaffected by roughness geometry.

This work provides valuable insights into passive flow control strategies for STBLIs, which are critical phenomena in high-speed flight. Understanding how wall roughness can modify turbulence and shock dynamics offers potential avenues for mitigating adverse effects in supersonic and hypersonic vehicle designs, particularly in areas prone to strong shock interactions.

This paper review was generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash and curated by AeroSentinel v2.5.0.

Reference

  1. Wencan Wu, L. Laguarda, Davide Modesti et al., “Passive control of shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction via ridge-type roughness,” Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 2026-02-23. Link
